claims.text: What the strip looks like Orthodromic AVRT: a narrow-QRS tachycardia — down the AV node and His-Purkinje system, back up the accessory pathway — with the P wave shortly after the QRS (short RP).
claims.quote: Narrow QRS Tachycardia: Orthodromic Atrioventricular Reentrant Tachycardia Using an Accessory AV Connection in Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome Activation is as follows: atrioventricular node, His-Purkinje system, ventricle, accessory connection, atria. The P wave occurs shortly after the QRS complex; it is a short RP interval tachycardia (RP < PR).

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) P waves: always after the QRS in orthodromic AVRT
claims.quote: P waves always follow the QRS complex in orthodromic typical atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia using an accessory AV connection as in WPW syndrome.

claims.text: QRS: wide in antidromic AVRT, when the ventricles are activated down the accessory pathway
claims.quote: Wide QRS complexes also result from activation of the ventricles exclusively down an accessory AV connection in antidromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia or dual accessory connection atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia.

claims.text: A wide-complex tachycardia not known to be supraventricular must be treated as VT
claims.quote: If a wide-complex tachycardia is not known to be supraventricular in origin, it must be treated acutely as ventricular tachycardia.

claims.text: Between episodes (manifest WPW): short PR, wide QRS with a delta wave, secondary repolarization changes
claims.quote: Classic (manifest) Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is due to an accessory atrioventricular connection that produces a prototypical ECG consisting of a short PR interval, a wide QRS complex with an initial slurred component (delta wave), and secondary repolarization changes

claims.text: AF with WPW: rate > 200, irregular, wide QRS complexes that change in shape; the axis stays stable (unlike polymorphic VT)
claims.quote: Rate > 200 bpm Irregular rhythm Wide QRS complexes due to abnormal ventricular depolarisation via accessory pathway QRS complexes change in shape and morphology Axis remains stable, unlikely polymorphic VT

claims.text: Causes (mechanism and diagnoses) Mechanism (orthodromic): the impulse goes down the AV node, back up the accessory pathway to the atria, then around again
claims.quote: When antegrade conduction through the AV node is sufficiently slow, it can find the distal accessory AV connection ready to conduct, but in the retrograde direction. When this retrograde accessory AC connection transmission finds the atria and, subsequently, the AV node ready to conduct again in the antegrade direction, around-and-around atrioventricular reentry occurs.

claims.text: WPW (manifest or concealed) is the most common accessory-pathway PSVT
claims.quote: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, whether manifest or concealed, is the most common accessory pathway PSVT.

claims.text: AF occurs in up to 20% of WPW patients; the pathway conducts it straight to the ventricles, bypassing the AV node, and rapid rates can degenerate to VT or VF
claims.quote: Atrial fibrillation can occur in up to 20% of patients with Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome (WPW) The accessory pathway allows for rapid conduction directly to the ventricles bypassing the AV node Rapid ventricular rates may result in degeneration to VT or VF

claims.text: Symptoms Episodes of sudden-onset, sudden-offset, rapid, regular palpitations, often with dyspnea, chest discomfort or light-headedness
claims.quote: They typically have episodes of sudden-onset, sudden-offset, rapid, regular palpitations often associated with symptoms of hemodynamic compromise (eg, dyspnea, chest discomfort, light-headedness).

claims.text: Rapidly conducted AF or 1:1 flutter: hemodynamic compromise and syncope are more common; rapidly conducted AF can induce VF and sudden death (about 1%, more likely in adolescence)
claims.quote: Patients with WPW syndrome may also experience rapidly conducted supraventricular arrhythmias such as 1:1 conduction of atrial flutter or rapidly conducted atrial fibrillation wherein symptoms of hemodynamic compromise, including syncope are more common. Rapidly conducted atrial fibrillation may also induce ventricular fibrillation and sudden death. This risk is low (approximately 1%) but is more likely to occur in adolescence.

claims.text: Treatment Narrow, regular (orthodromic): vagal maneuvers, then AV node blockers — blocking one AV-node beat interrupts the circuit
claims.quote: AV node blockers are used if vagotonic maneuvers are ineffective and the QRS complex is narrow (indicating orthodromic conduction) and regular (indicating the episode is not atrial fibrillation); blocking conduction through the AV node for one beat interrupts the reentrant cycle.

claims.text: Wide-complex tachycardia not known to be PSVT: no AV nodal blockers; synchronized cardioversion, procainamide or amiodarone
claims.quote: Avoid AV nodal blockers for wide complex tachycardia not known to be PSVT; use synchronized cardioversion or procainamide or amiodarone.

claims.text: AF with WPW: no AV nodal blockers (adenosine, CCBs, beta blockers) — they can increase conduction down the pathway and precipitate VT or VF
claims.quote: Treatment with AV nodal blocking drugs e.g. adenosine, calcium-channel blockers, beta-blockers may increase conduction via the accessory pathway with a resultant increase in ventricular rate and possible degeneration into VT or VF

claims.text: AF with WPW: unstable → urgent synchronized DC cardioversion; stable → procainamide or ibutilide, though DC cardioversion may be preferred
claims.quote: In a haemodynamically unstable patient urgent synchronised DC cardioversion is required. Medical treatment options in a stable patient include procainamide or ibutilide, although DC cardioversion may be preferred

claims.text: Frequent or bothersome episodes: catheter ablation is preferred and usually curative
claims.quote: When episodes of reentrant (paroxysmal) supraventricular tachycardia are frequent or bothersome, transvenous catheter ablation is the preferred treatment and is usually curative
